transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Menon (CTO, Custodian), Hector Alvarez (Head of Infra), Sofia Ramos (Security PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, maybe rough):
- Purpose: scope POC for private networking + egress constraints, validate benchmarks and success criteria for Custodian Therapeutics pilot.
- High level: customer needs strict egress control (only to approved analytics endpoints), region-lockdown for EU workloads, and audit logs to be retained 1 year. Seeking 4-week pilot with bench results.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we scheduled 50 minutes, i'll kick off, quick intro - i'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions eng, hi liam.
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: hey all, quick wave, ready to dig in.
[00:11] Dr. Priya Menon: thanks maya, appreciate it. we—i'm priya, CTO at custodian, we run sensitive imaging pipelines and can't have PHI leaving eu regions.
[00:20] Hector Alvarez: hector here, infra lead. main ask: we need absolute control over outbound egress, and audit trail for every request. also throughput should support 200 concurrent inference sessions at peak.
[00:31] Sofia Ramos: hi—so security, quick note: must use our KMS for key operations, logs must go to our splunk instance in eu-west-1, and third-party analytics is permitted only to a pinned CIDR.
[00:44] Maya Chen: great — that's really helpful. quick sanity check: are you leaning toward Redwoods Private (vpc/on-prem) or Dedicated? or open to hosted if we can enforce egress?
[00:54] Dr. Priya Menon: preference is Private control plane in our VPC. we want the control plane to be managed but the data path must never leave our network except to allowed analytics destinations.
[01:05] Liam O'Connor: ok, so two main connectivity patterns we usually discuss: VPC peering (low-latency, but needs route tables and peering acceptance) vs AWS PrivateLink (endpoint-based, tighter egress control). both can be configured for region locking.
[01:20] Hector Alvarez: our security team prefers endpoint-based patterns because peering creates broad route access. we worry about lateral movement.
[01:27] Maya Chen: understood. PrivateLink gives you explicit endpoint IPs and is easier for egress filtering — you can limit NAT/GW rules to those endpoints. downside is more endpoints to manage per region.
[01:38] Dr. Priya Menon: can you explain resume of traffic flow if we do PrivateLink? like training vs inference calls, kv cache, telemetry?
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: sure — with PrivateLink, traffic goes to an interface endpoint inside your VPC, it never traverses public internet, Redwood's carrier nets route to that endpoint. KV cache (our prefix cache) can be co-located on the same private path; we can also offer a caching proxy inside your subnet to further reduce outbound. telemetry and audit logs are pushed via a secure syslog or direct forwarder to your splunk — but that depends on whether you want us to push logs or for you to pull them.
[02:05] Sofia Ramos: we need push with mutual TLS and our certs, no pulling. also log retention—1 year, immutable if possible.
[02:12] Maya Chen: we can support mTLS for log endpoints and preserve append-only logs; we'll call out retention in the runbook.
[02:17] Hector Alvarez: about egress: we have an internal analytics collector at 10.11.22.45/32 — only that CIDR should be allowed. all other destinations blocked. we also have a third-party monitoring vendor whose IPs are known.
[02:28] Liam O'Connor: that's doable. typical pattern: Redwood Private deploys a VPC endpoint inside your account; we present a set of fixed outbound IPs to you (or we fit into your NAT egress rules). For PrivateLink, we hand you ENIs and those are static from AWS perspective.
[02:40] Dr. Priya Menon: latency SLA — we need 95th percentile under 200ms for a 1k-token generation workload. is that realistic inside-private?
[02:49] Liam O'Connor: yes, for smaller models and with kv cache warming that's achievable. for larger context lengths or big LLMs you may need dedicated capacity or quantized models. we can design the bench to reflect your real payloads — images-plus-text, i assume?
[03:00] Dr. Priya Menon: mainly text + extracted metadata, avg prompt 450 tokens, responses ~600 tokens. concurrency spikes to 200 for short windows.
[03:10] Maya Chen: perfect. our bench proposal — synthetic load that mirrors: avg payload 450/600, 200 concurrency spike, long-tail 99th percentile checks, and a separate cold-start scenario measuring kv cache impact. target success: p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms, throughput sustaining 200 concurrent sessions with median latency < 120ms during steady state.
[03:30] Hector Alvarez: p99 350 is okay as long as we have predictable cost. what about token cost and batching? we can't have spikes racking up cost.
[03:37] Liam O'Connor: we will include batching profiles, smart batching to balance latency and token cost, and quantify unit economics in the bench. we'll surface recommended quantization settings (8-bit, 4-bit) and model variants.
[03:49] Sofia Ramos: compliance questions — SSO/SAML for console, RBAC for team members, audit push to splunk with fields: request_id, model_version, user_id, prompt_hash. can you provide schema?
[04:02] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share the log schema. RBAC and SAML supported in Private.
[04:07] Dr. Priya Menon: timeline — we want results in 4 weeks ideally. week1: network setup and cert exchange, week2: smoke bench and instrumentation, week3: full bench, week4: wrap and findings. any blockers?
[04:18] Liam O'Connor: that timeline is achievable. main blocker is access to your VPC and a short maintenance window to accept PrivateLink endpoints, plus KMS access for env config.
[04:26] Hector Alvarez: KMS—must be our CMK, usable by Redwood with a cross-account grant that can be revoked.
[04:33] Maya Chen: we support using customer-managed keys and an auditable grant pattern. we'll document grant lifecycle.
[04:38] Hector Alvarez: also, can you guarantee no egress to non-approved AWS regions? we need region locking to eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 only.
[04:46] Liam O'Connor: yes, we can pin the deployment to specific regions and disallow cross-region fallbacks in the routing policy. fallback policies can be disabled for the POC.
[04:53] Sofia Ramos: what about emergency failover if a region has an outage—will you fall back to us-east-1? that's a dealbreaker if it happens without explicit approval.
[05:01] Maya Chen: for the POC we can enforce no automatic cross-region fallback; any failover would be manual and documented in the runbook.
[05:07] Dr. Priya Menon: bench specifics — i want to see: 1) steady-state 8-hour sim, 2) 10-minute spike test to 200 concurrency, 3) cold-start ramp test, and 4) end-to-end telemetry sample for 5% of requests.
[05:20] Liam O'Connor: noted. we'll provide scripts (k6/locust) and a bench matrix with exact payloads. we'll push metrics: latency distribution, tokens per second, GPU utilization, error rates, and cost estimate per 1M tokens.
[05:33] Hector Alvarez: any concerns about KV cache warm-up when you run bench across our PrivateLink? do you need pre-warmed state?
[05:40] Liam O'Connor: better to pre-warm with synthetic prefixes for the cold-to-warm tests; we'll coordinate keys we use so you can audit contents. cache can be local to the enclave so it doesn't leave your VPC.
[05:50] Sofia Ramos: on logging — we need immutable logs for 1 year; can Redwood produce a signed, tamper-evident export weekly?
[05:59] Maya Chen: we can produce signed weekly bundles and push to your S3 with write-once rules, plus forward to Splunk with mTLS. we'll include the signed hash manifest.
[06:09] Dr. Priya Menon: pricing—your AE mentioned committed capacity vs pay-as-you-go. because of our volume projections, reserved capacity might be better but we want a POC-friendly short commitment.
[06:18] Maya Chen: we typically do a 1-month reserved trial for pilots with a consumption cap; we'll propose a pilot pricing line item that can convert to quarterly reserved if successful.
[06:26] Hector Alvarez: ok. can you also show how network ACLs will look in our account? like a minimal set of rules we need to open.
[06:33] Liam O'Connor: yes — we'll produce a terraform snippet with the required endpoint security group, NACLs, and route table entries for PrivateLink.
[06:40] Dr. Priya Menon: great. any red flags from your side?
[06:44] Liam O'Connor: only that we need early access to the splunk endpoint cert and the CIDR of your analytics collector. if those are delayed, bench will shift.
[06:52] Sofia Ramos: we'll get cert and CIDRs today.
[06:55] Maya Chen: perfect. recap: redwood delivers bench plan and runbook, includes PrivateLink architecture, mTLS log push, KMS grant instructions, terraform snippet, and pilot pricing by monday. customer provides CIDRs, splunk cert, and confirms target regions by thursday. schedule bench run next week 60–90 min.
[07:15] Dr. Priya Menon: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:17] Hector Alvarez: thanks.
[07:18] Sofia Ramos: bye.

Meeting end.
